title: The Lament for Saul and Jonathan
subtitle: 2 Samuel 1
description: A messenger, a crown, an execution, and the Song of the Bow taught to all Judah.
paragraphs: David came home to a burned town. He had wept until he had no strength left to weep, then inquired of God, then ridden south and taken everything back from the Amalekites who raided Ziklag, down to the last wife and the last spoon. Now he was back in the ashes, rebuilding, and he had been there two days when the news he had been outrunning for years finally caught up with him. On the third day a man arrived from Saul's camp with his clothes torn and dust on his head, the uniform of a bearer of disaster, and he fell to the ground before David and did homage. David asked where he had come from, and the man said he had escaped from the Israelite camp. David asked the only question that mattered: what was the outcome? The answer came in three strokes, each one worse. The troops had fled from the battle. Many of them had fallen and died. And Saul and his son Jonathan were also dead.

David did not take a stranger's word for the death of a king. He asked the young man how he knew, and the young man told a story built to please him. He said he had happened to be on Mount Gilboa, and there was Saul, leaning on his spear, with the chariots and the cavalry closing in on him. Saul had turned and seen him and called out, and asked who he was, and he had answered that he was an Amalekite. Then Saul had begged him: "Stand over me and kill me, for agony has seized me, but my life still lingers." So he had stood over the king and killed him, he said, because he knew that after he had fallen he could not survive. And he had taken the crown from Saul's head and the band from his arm, and here they were, brought to his lord. Any reader coming straight from the last book holds a second version of that death in the same hands: there, Saul fell on his own sword after his armor-bearer refused him, and no Amalekite stood over him. This book does not stop to reconcile the two accounts. It lets the man's story stand as the story he told David, and everything that follows in the chapter turns on what he said, and on the crown in his hands.

What the messenger expected was a reward. What he got was grief, total and immediate. David took hold of his own clothes and tore them, and every man with him did the same, and they mourned and wept and fasted until evening. Note the list of the dead they grieved: for Saul, and for his son Jonathan, and for the people of the LORD and the house of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword. The king who had hunted David for years, who had thrown spears at him and chased him through two countries, was mourned by David's whole camp until dark, without qualification. Only then, after the fasting, did David turn back to the young man and ask where he was from. The answer sealed his fate: he was the son of a foreigner, an Amalekite. David asked him one question: "Why were you not afraid to lift your hand to destroy the LORD's anointed?" The man's own story was the whole case against him. He had come expecting that David hated Saul, and he had built his tale on that arithmetic, perhaps shaping it as he went. But David's arithmetic about the anointed king had never changed, not in the cave at En-gedi, not in the camp at Hachilah, and it did not change now that the king was dead and the crown was in the room. David summoned one of his young men and ordered the execution, and the verdict he pronounced was drawn from the man's own mouth: "Your blood be on your own head because your own mouth has testified against you". He had condemned himself with his own boast: "I killed the LORD's anointed."

Then David did the thing that has carried his name down the centuries as surely as the giant did. He took up a lament for Saul and Jonathan, and he ordered that the sons of Judah be taught it, the Song of the Bow, written, the text says, in the Book of Jashar, the same lost book that once preserved Joshua's long day. It is a song with no gloating in it and no mention of God settling any scores for David. It opens in ruin: "Your glory, O Israel, lies slain on your heights. How the mighty have fallen!" Its first instinct is protection of the dead king's honor, that the news be kept from Israel's enemies: "Tell it not in Gath; proclaim it not in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice". It curses the ground where the king died, the mountains of Gilboa, calling down a sky with no dew or rain on them, because there the shield of the mighty was defiled. And then it does something only David in that generation would have done: it praises Saul at full strength, alongside Jonathan, as a pair bound in life and in death. "Saul and Jonathan, beloved and delightful in life, were not divided in death. They were swifter than eagles; they were stronger than lions." It thanks Saul for Israel's daughters' scarlet and gold, the prosperity of his reign remembered by the very man that reign spent its last years hunting.

The lament narrows at the end to one name. "How the mighty have fallen in the thick of battle! Jonathan lies slain on your heights." Then the most famous sentence David ever spoke about another person: "I grieve for you, Jonathan, my brother. You were delightful to me; your love to me was extraordinary, surpassing the love of women." The prince who had handed David his robe and his weapons, who had sworn him a covenant and accepted second place in a kingdom he would never see, was dead on the same hill as his father, and David's song gives the last word neither to kingship nor to victory but to the refrain that has run under the whole chapter like a drumbeat, spoken a third and final time: "How the mighty have fallen, and the weapons of war have perished!" The crown was in David's hands now. The throne stood empty. And the first public act of the man who would take it was a song for the two men whose deaths had emptied it, taught to all Judah so that no one would be allowed to remember that day cheaply.

title: King of Judah, War with the House of Saul
subtitle: 2 Samuel 2
description: Hebron, the pool of Gibeon, Asahel's death, Abner's defection and murder, and a throne left open.
paragraphs: The lament was sung. Then David did what he had done at every hinge of his life since the cave of Adullam: he inquired of the LORD. Should he go up to one of the towns of Judah? The answer was yes. Where? To Hebron. So the fugitive went up out of the ashes of Ziklag with his two wives, Ahinoam and Abigail, and his six hundred men with their households, and settled in the towns around Hebron, Abraham's old city. And the men of Judah came and anointed David king over the house of Judah. It was a partial crown, one tribe out of twelve, and David's first act with it tells you the kind of king he meant to be. He was told it was the men of Jabesh-gilead who had buried Saul, the town across the Jordan that Saul had rescued in his first flush of kingship and that had now repaid the debt at the risk of their lives. David sent them a blessing in the name of the LORD and a promise in his own: because they had shown kindness to Saul their lord, the LORD would show them loving devotion and faithfulness, and David would show them the same favor. "Now then, be strong and courageous, for though Saul your lord is dead, the house of Judah has anointed me as their king." Before he fought the house of Saul, he honored the men who had buried its head.

But Saul had a son, and Saul had a general. Abner son of Ner, commander of Saul's army, took Ish-bosheth across the Jordan to Mahanaim and made him king over the north and east, over Gilead and Ephraim and Benjamin, over all Israel except Judah. Ish-bosheth was forty years old and reigned two years, though the war dragged on far longer than his reign, and the text gives the whole conflict its summary in a single sentence: the war between the house of Saul and the house of David was protracted, and David grew stronger and stronger, while the house of Saul grew weaker and weaker. Ish-bosheth was a king the way a flag is an army. Abner was the power, and everyone in both camps knew it.

The war's ugliest day began as a game. The two armies met at the pool of Gibeon and sat down on opposite sides of the water, and Abner proposed to Joab, David's commander, that the young men get up and compete before them. Twelve against twelve came forward, and each man grabbed his opponent by the head and drove his sword into his opponent's side, and all twenty-four fell together in a place named ever after the Field of Blades. Then the real battle joined, and Abner's Israelites broke and ran. Among David's men that day were the three sons of Zeruiah, David's nephews: Joab, Abishai, and Asahel, the youngest, fleet of foot like a wild gazelle. Asahel fixed on Abner himself and ran him down and would not turn aside to the right or to the left. Twice Abner warned him off, and the second warning was almost a plea, because Abner could see the whole future in this chase: "Stop chasing me. Why should I strike you to the ground? How could I show my face to your brother Joab?" Asahel refused to turn away, and Abner drove the butt of his spear backward into his stomach, and the young man fell dead on the spot, and every soldier who came to the place where he lay stopped and stood still. Joab and Abishai hunted Abner until sunset, when Abner rallied his Benjamites on a hilltop and called across the dark the truest words spoken in that war: "Must the sword devour forever? Do you not realize that this will only end in bitterness?" Joab answered that had Abner not spoken, the pursuit would have run till morning, and he blew the ram's horn, and the armies separated. Joab counted his missing: nineteen men, and Asahel. They buried Asahel in his father's tomb in Bethlehem and marched all night, reaching Hebron at daybreak. But the account between Joab and Abner was not closed by any trumpet. It had merely been opened.

While the war ground on, sons were born to David in Hebron, and the narrator lists six of them by six mothers in the flat tone of a census. Hold the names, because this book will: the firstborn Amnon, and the third son Absalom, and the fourth Adonijah. The succession that would tear David's house apart was being born in the same years he was winning it. The end of the war, when it came, began not with a battle but with an insult. Ish-bosheth accused Abner of taking Rizpah, Saul's concubine, a charge that amounted to claiming the dead king's throne rights. Abner exploded. All this time he had been loyal to the house of Saul, he said, and now he was accused over a woman; so he swore to do for David what the LORD had sworn to him, to transfer the kingdom from the house of Saul and set David's throne over Israel and Judah from Dan to Beersheba. Ish-bosheth did not dare say another word to him. The king of Israel had just learned who his king was.

Abner's messengers came to David proposing a covenant, and David agreed, with one requirement that reached back across the whole story: Abner was not to appear before him unless he brought Michal, Saul's daughter, David's first wife, the woman who had lowered him in a basket through a window and saved his life, whom Saul had since given to another man as a political erasure. She was taken from her husband Paltiel, who followed her weeping all the way to Bahurim until Abner told him to go back, and he went. Abner then did the politics, conferring with the elders of Israel and with his own tribe of Benjamin, and came to Hebron with twenty men to a feast in David's house, and left in peace with a promise to gather all Israel to the king. Hours later Joab returned from a raid and learned that Abner had been in Hebron and had been sent away in peace, and he went to the king in fury: Abner had come to deceive him, to track his movements. Then, without David's knowledge, Joab sent messengers to recall Abner, and at the gateway of Hebron he pulled him aside as if for a private word and stabbed him in the stomach. The text names the motive without varnish: Abner died on account of the blood of Joab's brother Asahel.

David's response was a campaign of innocence conducted in public. He declared himself and his kingdom forever guiltless before the LORD of Abner's blood, and laid a curse on the house of Joab with the particularity of a curse meant to be quoted. He ordered Joab himself and all the people to tear their clothes and put on sackcloth and walk in mourning, and the king walked behind the bier, and wept aloud at the tomb, and sang a lament whose sting was that Abner had died unbound and unresisting: "As a man falls before the wicked, so also you fell." He refused food until sundown under oath. And all the people took note, and all Israel was convinced that the king had no part in the murder of Abner. Then David said the sentence that hangs over the rest of his reign, to his own servants, about the nephews he could neither punish nor dismiss: "And I am weak this day, though anointed as king, and these men, the sons of Zeruiah, are too fierce for me. May the LORD repay the evildoer according to his evil!" A king who cannot bring his own commander to justice has announced the limit of his crown, and this book remembers it.

What remained of the house of Saul collapsed within days. When Ish-bosheth heard that Abner was dead, he lost courage, and two of his own raiding captains, Rechab and Baanah, came into his house in the heat of the day while he slept his midday sleep, stabbed him, cut off his head, and carried it all night down the Arabah road to Hebron, expecting the same reward the Amalekite had expected. David answered them with the Amalekite's story. When a man told him Saul was dead, thinking he brought good news, David had seized him and put him to death at Ziklag; that was his reward for his news. "As surely as the LORD lives, who has redeemed my life from all distress", how much more would he require the blood of wicked men who had killed a righteous man in his own house and on his own bed? The brothers were executed, their bodies displayed by the pool in Hebron, and Ish-bosheth's head was buried with honor in Abner's tomb. On the way to that tomb the narrator pauses for four verses of pure setup, and they matter more than the battle reports: Jonathan son of Saul had a son who was lame in his feet. He was five years old when the news came from Jezreel, and his nurse had fled with him and dropped him in the hurry, and he was lame from that day. His name was Mephibosheth. The house of Saul now consisted of a dead king, a murdered pretender, and a crippled boy in hiding. The throne of Israel stood open.

title: King Over All Israel, and Jerusalem
subtitle: 2 Samuel 5
description: The tribes covenant at Hebron, a taunted city taken, and the ark brought up past Uzzah's fall.
paragraphs: Seven and a half years after Hebron, the whole nation came to David there. All the tribes of Israel stood before him with a claim and a memory. The claim was kinship: here we are, your own flesh and blood. The memory was the open secret of Saul's reign, that even while Saul was king it was David who had led Israel out and brought them back. And they quoted the promise over him, the word spoken years before by Samuel's God: "You will shepherd My people Israel, and you will be ruler over them." So the elders of Israel came to the king at Hebron, and David made a covenant with them before the LORD, a king bound by agreement and not merely by conquest, and they anointed him king over Israel. He was thirty years old when he became king, and he reigned forty years, seven and a half in Hebron over Judah and thirty-three in Jerusalem over all Israel and Judah. The shepherd of Bethlehem had the whole flock now. What he needed was a capital that belonged to no tribe, and he knew exactly where it was.

Jerusalem sat on the border between Judah and Benjamin, held by the Jebusites, unconquered since Joshua's day, so secure on its rock that its defenders taunted David from the walls: he would never get in; even the blind and the lame could repel him. The taunt became the city's epitaph. David took the fortress of Zion by its water shaft, the hidden artery the Jebusites had trusted, and the fortress became the City of David. He built it up from the terraces inward, and the text's verdict on these years is the sentence that stands under his whole reign: David became greater and greater, for the LORD God of Hosts was with him. Hiram king of Tyre, the great trading power on the coast, read the situation correctly and sent cedar logs and carpenters and masons, and a palace rose in the captured city. And David understood, the narrator says, that the LORD had established him as king over Israel and had exalted his kingdom not for David's sake but for the sake of His people Israel. It is the healthiest sentence in the book about the use of power, and it comes early, before the book tests it.

The Philistines also read the situation. Twice they came up in force into the Valley of Rephaim to end the reunified kingdom before it set, and twice the new king did the old thing he had learned in the wilderness: he inquired of the LORD. The first time, the answer was to go straight up, and David crushed them at Baal-perazim and named the place for the breakthrough: "Like a bursting flood, the LORD has burst out against my enemies before me." The second time, the answer was different instructions for the same enemy in the same valley: do not march straight up; circle behind them; wait for the sound of marching in the tops of the balsam trees, for that would mean the LORD had gone out before him. David obeyed the stranger order as exactly as he had obeyed the simple one, and struck the Philistines from Gibeon to Gezer. Israel's ancient enemy would raid again, but it would never again rule the story. The wars of survival were over. What remained was the harder work of building a kingdom that could hold God at its center without mishandling Him.

That work began with the ark. The ark of God had rested for decades in the house of Abinadab at Kiriath-jearim, ever since Beth-shemesh sent it away, and David determined to bring it up to his new capital with the whole nation watching. Thirty thousand chosen men assembled, and the ark was set on a new cart, drawn by oxen, guided by Abinadab's sons Uzzah and Ahio, and David and all Israel celebrated before the LORD with every instrument they had. A new cart was how the Philistines had once sent the ark home. It was efficient, and it was festive, and at the threshing floor of Nacon the oxen stumbled, and Uzzah reached out and took hold of the ark of God to steady it, and the anger of the LORD burned against him, and God struck him down on the spot for his irreverence, and he died there beside the ark. The text gives no softening and no explanation beyond the word irreverence: the holiest object in Israel was not cargo, and a well-meant hand was still a hand laid on what God had said was untouchable. David's anger came first, hot at the LORD who had burst forth against Uzzah the way He had burst forth against the Philistines, and David named the place Perez-uzzah, the bursting against Uzzah. Then the anger cooled into the truer emotion: that day David feared the LORD, and asked the question the whole chapter exists to ask: "How can the ark of the LORD ever come to me?" He would not move it. The ark went aside, into the house of a man named Obed-edom the Gittite, a foreigner by his name, a Gathite living in Israel, and it stayed there three months. And the LORD blessed Obed-edom and all his household, because of the ark of God.

The blessing was the report that changed David's mind, and the second procession was built on what the first had taught. This time there was no cart. The ark was carried, as it was made to be carried, and when the bearers had advanced six paces David sacrificed an ox and a fattened calf, sealing the road in worship from its first step. And David wore a linen ephod, dressed not as a king presiding but as a servant attending, and he danced with all his might before the LORD while the ark came up with shouting and the sound of the ram's horn. In a window above the street stood Michal, Saul's daughter, restored to David by treaty after her years with Paltiel, and she looked down and saw the king of Israel leaping and dancing before the LORD, stripped of every royal dignity, indistinguishable from the servants around the ark. And she despised him in her heart. The daughter of the first king watched the second king make himself small before God, and read it only as shame.

She met him at his own door with the shame spelled out, dressed in the politeness of a court and the contempt of a house that had lost everything: how the king of Israel had distinguished himself today, uncovering himself before the maidservants of his subjects like a vulgar person. David's answer reached past her to the whole history between their houses. It was before the LORD that he had danced, he told her, the LORD who chose him over her father and over all his house and appointed him ruler over the LORD's people Israel. "I will celebrate before the LORD, and I will humiliate and humble myself even more than this. Yet I will be honored by the maidservants of whom you have spoken." It is a complete exchange: her standard was the dignity of Saul's court; his standard was the God who had replaced that court. The book closes the scene and, in a sense, the house of Saul itself with one flat sentence, delivered without comment and heavy with it: Michal the daughter of Saul had no children to the day of her death. The ark was in the City of David, in a tent David had pitched for it. The king had a palace of cedar. And that contrast, a housed king and a tented God, is where the next episode begins.

title: The Promise to David's House
subtitle: 2 Samuel 7
description: A king who would build God a house receives a house instead, and the wars that followed it.
paragraphs: The wars paused, and the king sat in his new palace with an uncomfortable comparison on his mind. The ark had come up into the City of David rejoicing, and it rested in a tent David had pitched, while David lived behind cedar paneling that Tyrian carpenters had fitted. He said it to Nathan the prophet, who appears in the story here for the first time: "Here I am, living in a house of cedar, while the ark of God remains in a tent." It was a builder's conscience speaking, and Nathan answered like a man certain he knew God's mind because the plan was obviously good: go and do all that is in your heart, for the LORD is with you. That night the word of the LORD came to Nathan and reversed his advice completely. The prophet who had blessed the project in the afternoon had to return in the morning and unbless it, and the message he carried became the load-bearing wall of the whole Bible.

It began as a refusal wrapped in God's own history. Was David the one to build Him a house? God had not dwelt in a house from the Exodus to that day; He had moved about with a tent as His dwelling, journeying with Israel, and in all those journeys He had never once asked any leader why they had not built Him a house of cedar. The tent had never been a problem to the God who chose it. Then the message turned, and the refusal disclosed itself as the smaller half of the exchange. God rehearsed David's life back to him: He had taken him from the pasture, from following the flock, to be ruler over His people Israel; He had been with him wherever he went and cut off his enemies; He would make his name like the greatest in the land and plant His people in a place of their own, disturbed no more. And then the sentence that turns the chapter, and the kingship, inside out. David had proposed to build God a house. "The LORD declares to you that He Himself will establish a house for you." House was the word in play, and God took it up and made it mean a dynasty. When David's days were fulfilled and he rested with his fathers, God would raise up his descendant after him, from his own body, and establish his kingdom. That son would build a house for God's Name, the building David wanted to build, reassigned to the next generation. And the throne of his kingdom would be established forever.

The oracle held a father's terms alongside the forever. "I will be his Father, and he will be My son. When he does wrong, I will discipline him with the rod of men and with the blows of the sons of men." Discipline, real and painful, was written into the covenant in advance. What was written out of it was removal. "But My loving devotion will never be removed from him as I removed it from Saul, whom I removed from before you." Saul's line had been cut off for disobedience; David's line would be disciplined for it and kept. The promise closed with the words that Israel and the church after it would build on for a thousand years: "Your house and kingdom will endure forever before Me, and your throne will be established forever." Nathan relayed all of it, every word, and the prophet who had once run ahead of God's answer now simply carried God's answer, which proved to be far larger than the question.

David's response is the longest prayer of his life that the books preserve, and its first note is not ambition but scale. He went in and sat before the LORD, a king sitting down in the tent like a servant, and said: "Who am I, O Lord GOD, and what is my house, that You have brought me this far?" He marveled that God had treated a shepherd's family line as the material of forever, and that God had spoken not only of David's lifetime but of the distant future of his house as though it were a settled thing. "What more can David say to You? For You know Your servant, O Lord GOD." The prayer widened from his own house to Israel's: who was like this people, the one nation on earth God had gone out to redeem for Himself, driving out nations and their gods before them? And then, remarkably, the prayer did the boldest thing a prayer can do with a promise: it asked God to keep it. Confirm forever the word You have spoken concerning Your servant and his house; do as You have promised. David had found the courage to pray this prayer, he said, precisely because God had revealed the promise to him. The chapter ends with the house of David blessed by a word, not yet by a single stone of the temple David had imagined, and the king who wanted to give God a building went back to his palace having received a bloodline instead.

What follows in chapter 8 reads almost like the oracle being cashed in real time, and the narrator keeps a running refrain under the campaign reports: the LORD made David victorious wherever he went. David defeated the Philistines and subdued them for good, taking their chief city from them. He defeated Moab and subjected it, measuring its soldiers with a cord in a grim accounting the text reports without comment, two lengths for death and one for life, and Moab brought tribute. He shattered Hadadezer of Zobah on the Euphrates frontier, hamstringing the chariot horses, broke the Arameans of Damascus who came to help him, and planted garrisons in Damascus itself. The gold shields of Hadadezer's officers and a fortune in bronze came to Jerusalem, and when King Toi of Hamath sent gifts of silver and gold and bronze in gratitude, David dedicated all of it to the LORD, storing up the temple he would never build out of the spoils of the wars he had been given. Eighteen thousand Edomites fell in the Valley of Salt, and Edom came under garrisons too. The map of David's kingdom at its height ran from the Euphrates to the edge of Egypt, and the chapter closes not with conquest but with administration: David reigned over all Israel and administered justice and righteousness for all his people, with Joab over the army, Zadok and Ahimelech as priests, a recorder, a scribe, Benaiah over the king's foreign bodyguard, and David's sons as priestly leaders. Ahimelech's name in that list carries a whole history: he was the son of Abiathar, the lone survivor of Nob, whose murdered father had fed David the holy bread. The fugitive's priest now stood in the king's court. The kingdom was at rest, its house promised forever, its table about to be tested by a question David asked about a crippled boy hiding across the Jordan.

title: Kindness for Jonathan's Sake
subtitle: 2 Samuel 9
description: A crippled prince seated at the king's table, and a kindness across the border answered with humiliation and war.
paragraphs: At the height of the kingdom, David asked a question that reached backward instead of forward: "Is there anyone left from the house of Saul to whom I can show kindness for the sake of Jonathan?" Kings in that world did not ask that question. Kings asked it as a targeting exercise, to find the surviving claimants and end them. David asked it as a debt. He had sworn a covenant to Jonathan at the stone Ezel and again in the wilderness of Ziph, kindness to Jonathan's house forever, and a covenant in these books is not a memory, it is a bill that comes due. A servant of Saul's house named Ziba was summoned, a steward of the old regime with fifteen sons and twenty servants of his own, and the king put the question to him in its full form: was there anyone left of the house of Saul to whom he could show the kindness of God? Ziba's answer was careful and small. There was still a son of Jonathan, he said, who was lame in both feet. He gave the disability before he gave the man.

The boy from the narrator's aside in the war years was in Lo-debar, a place whose name suggests nowhere, east of the Jordan, sheltered in the house of Machir son of Ammiel. He had been five when the news of Gilboa reached Jezreel and his nurse dropped him in the flight, and he had lived ever since as the hidden remnant of a fallen dynasty, which in that century meant living as a man waiting to be found by the wrong king. David had him brought. When Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, the son of Saul, came into the presence of the man who had replaced his grandfather, he fell facedown in reverence, in terror or submission or both, and David called him by name, and he answered as a man answering for his life. David's first words to him were the covenant paying out: "Do not be afraid," and then the promise itself: "for surely I will show you kindness for the sake of your father Jonathan. I will restore to you all the land of your grandfather Saul, and you will always eat at my table." Not a pension. A seat. Mephibosheth bowed and answered with the vocabulary of a man who had priced his own worth in hiding: "What is your servant, that you should show regard for a dead dog like me?" David did not argue with the valuation. He simply arranged the facts against it: Saul's whole estate restored, Ziba and his sons and servants ordered to farm it and bring in the harvest for their master's grandson, and Mephibosheth himself placed permanently at the king's table in Jerusalem, eating, the text says, like one of the king's own sons. The chapter says it twice, and ends by saying the quiet part last, as this book loves to do: he lived in Jerusalem, because he always ate at the king's table, and he was lame in both feet. Grace in this story does not fix the lameness. It seats the lame man at the table anyway, every day, for life. It is the purest act of David's reign, and the narrative will not let it rest there, because Ziba has now been introduced, with his twenty servants and his careful answers, and Ziba will be back.

Kindness across a border fared worse. The king of the Ammonites died, and David sent servants to console his son Hanun, because Nahash had once shown David kindness, another old debt honored. Hanun's princes read the embassy as espionage, comforters sent to spy out the city for overthrow, and Hanun chose the reading that humiliated Jerusalem: he seized David's envoys, shaved off half of each man's beard, cut their garments off at the hips, and sent them home in disgrace. In that culture a beard was a man's honor worn on his face, and the half-shaved, half-dressed envoys were a declaration of contempt meant to be unanswerable. David's handling of his shamed men is worth noticing in a book that will soon show his handling of other men's wives and lives: he sent word to meet them on the road and told them to stay in Jericho until their beards grew back, and then return. He absorbed the insult's cost himself rather than parade their shame through his capital.

The Ammonites knew what they had done and bought an army: twenty thousand Aramean foot soldiers from Beth-rehob and Zobah, a thousand from the king of Maacah, twelve thousand from Tob. Joab marched out with the whole army of the mighty men and found the enemy arranged in two forces, Ammonites at their city gate and Arameans in the open country, with Israel caught between. Joab split his command on the spot, taking the best of Israel against the Arameans and giving Abishai the rest against Ammon, and the brothers made the pact that defines them at their best: whichever front broke first, the other would come to its rescue. Then Joab gave the order that has been quoted by soldiers ever since, and it is worth hearing whole, because it is this book's theology of courage in one breath: "Be strong and let us fight bravely for our people and for the cities of our God. May the LORD do what is good in His sight." Effort at full stretch, outcome surrendered. The Arameans fled before Joab's charge; the Ammonites, seeing their hirelings run, fled before Abishai into their city; and the campaign ended, for the moment, with Joab back in Jerusalem.

It did not hold. The Arameans, shamed by the defeat, regrouped under Hadadezer, drawing fresh armies from beyond the Euphrates to Helam under their commander Shobach, and this time David did not delegate. He gathered all Israel, crossed the Jordan, and fought in person, and Israel routed them so completely that the kings subject to Hadadezer made peace and served Israel, and the Arameans were afraid to help the Ammonites anymore. Ammon stood alone behind the walls of its capital, Rabbah, and Israel's army settled into the siege that frames the next episode. Remember where the king is in this chapter: at the front, in person, crossing rivers to finish a war his enemy started. Remember it because chapter 11 opens with the same war, the same siege, and one devastating difference in where the king has chosen to be.

title: Bathsheba, and Nathan's Story
subtitle: 2 Samuel 11
description: A king who stayed home, a soldier who would not, a parable of a lamb, and a sentence on a house.
paragraphs: In the spring, at the time when kings march out to war, David sent Joab and the whole army of Israel to finish the siege of Rabbah, and David remained in Jerusalem. The sentence is the hinge of the book, and everything that follows swings on it. One evening the king got up from his bed and strolled on the roof of the palace, and from the roof he saw a woman bathing, a very beautiful woman. The seeing was chance. Nothing after it was. David sent and inquired about her, and the answer identified her completely, in a form that gave him every fact he needed to stop: this was Bathsheba, the daughter of Eliam and the wife of Uriah the Hittite. Uriah was no stranger. He was one of David's own mighty men, one of the Thirty, a Hittite who had bound his loyalty to Israel's king and Israel's God, and at that moment he was in the field at Rabbah, fighting David's war. David sent messengers and got her, and she came to him, and he slept with her, and she returned home. The text spends no words on her choices because the text assigns the agency where the power was: a king sends, and subjects come. Some weeks later Bathsheba sent the king a message of two words, and the whole architecture of the cover-up rose on them: "I am pregnant."

The cover-up began as hospitality. David ordered Joab to send Uriah home, received him warmly, asked after Joab and the troops and the progress of the war like a king honoring a soldier, and told him to go down to his house and wash his feet, with a present from the king trailing after him as a hint. Uriah left the palace and slept at its door with the king's servants, and did not go home. Reported to David, summoned back, he gave the answer that has judged his king in every century since: "The ark and Israel and Judah are dwelling in tents, and my master Joab and his soldiers are camped in the open field. How can I go to my house to eat and drink and sleep with my wife?" He swore by the king's own life that he would not do it. The foreign soldier held a standard of solidarity with men in tents that the anointed king, in his palace above the city, had already shrugged off, and he held it drunk as faithfully as sober: David kept him another day, fed him, got him drunk, and in the evening Uriah went out to his cot among the servants and still did not go home. The cover-up had met a man it could not move, so the cover-up became a murder, and a letter. In the morning David wrote to Joab and sent the letter by Uriah's own hand, the victim carrying his own death warrant in his saddlebag: "Put Uriah at the front of the fiercest battle; then withdraw from him, so that he may be struck down and killed." Joab obeyed, placing Uriah where he knew the strongest enemy soldiers were, and the men of the city came out and fought, and some of David's servants fell, good men whose names the book does not give, dying to complete an arrangement they knew nothing about, and Uriah the Hittite also died.

Joab's report to the king is a cold masterpiece of complicity. He scripted the messenger for the king's anger, anticipating the tactical complaint, and at the end of the script he placed the one sentence that would dissolve the anger: your servant Uriah the Hittite is dead as well. When the messenger delivered it, David answered with a proverb for a conscience: the sword devours one as well as another. The thing was done, wrapped, and filed. Bathsheba mourned her husband for the proper time, and when the mourning was over David had her brought to his house, and she became his wife and bore him a son. The book then closes the chapter with the sentence that the whole palace machinery had been built to avoid, delivered in the flattest voice in Scripture: "But the thing that David had done was evil in the sight of the LORD." The Psalter ties Psalm 51 to the interview that follows, David's own words after Nathan came to him; the song belongs to the doorway this chapter opens.

Then the LORD sent Nathan to David. The prophet who had once carried God's promise to this king now came carrying God's case against him, and he brought it as a story, because a king who could not see himself might still see a stranger. There were two men in a certain city, one rich and one poor. The rich man had herds beyond counting. The poor man had nothing except one small ewe lamb he had bought, which had grown up with him and his children, sharing his food, drinking from his cup, sleeping in his arms, like a daughter to him. A traveler came to the rich man, and the rich man, unwilling to take an animal of his own, took the poor man's lamb and prepared it for his guest. Nathan stopped. David detonated. He burned with anger against the man and swore by the living LORD that the man who did this deserved to die and would pay for the lamb four times over, because he had shown no pity. The outrage was genuine, which was the tragedy: the king's moral instincts were fully alive, aimed everywhere but at the mirror. Then Nathan said the four words that have echoed ever since: "You are that man!" And the indictment unrolled, in God's voice, through the whole history: I anointed you, I delivered you from Saul, I gave you his house and his kingdom, and if that had been too little I would have given you even more. Why have you despised the command of the LORD by doing evil in His sight? "You put Uriah the Hittite to the sword and took his wife as your own. You have slain him with the sword of the Ammonites." The sentence matched the crime's architecture: because David had done this in secret against another man's house, adversity would rise against him from his own house; what he did in darkness would be done to him in broad daylight before all Israel. And beneath the sentence the permanent clause: "Now, therefore, the sword will never depart from your house".

David's answer was five words and no excuses, no list of pressures, no Saul-style footnotes: "I have sinned against the LORD." Nathan answered on the spot: "The LORD has taken away your sin," and the limit came with it: "You will not die." Forgiveness, immediate and real. And consequence, immediate and real, in the same breath: nevertheless, the son born to him would surely die. Nathan went home, and the LORD struck the child, and David pleaded with God for the boy on the ground, fasting, lying in sackcloth through the night while the elders of his household stood over him unable to raise him. On the seventh day the child died, and the servants were afraid to tell the king, until David read their whispering correctly and asked them straight out, and they answered that he was dead. Then David did the thing that confused his whole court: he rose from the ground, washed, anointed himself, changed his clothes, went into the house of the LORD and worshiped, came home, and asked for food and ate. Asked to explain, he gave them his theology of grief in two sentences. While the child lived, he had fasted and wept, because who knows, the LORD might have been gracious and let him live. "But now that he is dead, why should I fast? Can I bring him back again? I will go to him, but he will not return to me." The pleading had been real hope, not theater, and when hope closed he worshiped and ate and comforted Bathsheba, and she bore another son, and they named him Solomon, and the LORD loved the child and sent word through Nathan to give him a second name, Jedidiah, beloved of the LORD. Meanwhile Joab finished the siege David's sin had interrupted, took the royal fortress and the water supply of Rabbah, and sent for the king to come and take the city himself, so that it would not be named after Joab. David went, and the crown of the Ammonite king, a talent of gold, was set on his head. The reign went on, blessed and sentenced at once. The sword that would never depart from his house was already being sharpened, and it was being sharpened, as promised, inside his own family.

title: Amnon and Absalom
subtitle: 2 Samuel 13
description: A sister wronged, a king's silence, two years of waiting, and a wise woman from Tekoa.
paragraphs: Nathan had said the sword would never depart from David's house, and the first stroke of it fell inside the family, in a story the narrator tells with unbearable exactness. Amnon, David's firstborn, fell sick with desire for his half-sister Tamar, the full sister of Absalom, a virgin of the king's household, and he had a friend, Jonadab, the king's nephew, a very shrewd man, who read his cousin's misery in a morning and happily supplied the engineering for it. Feign illness, Jonadab advised. When the king comes to see you, ask for Tamar to come and make cakes in your sight, so that you may eat from her hand. David, who had never learned to suspect his own house, sent the order himself: Tamar was to go to her brother's house and prepare a meal for him. She came and kneaded dough and made cakes in his sight and baked them, a sister's ordinary kindness performed in full view of the trap, and when she set the pan before him he refused to eat, and cleared the room. Then he told her to bring the food into the bedroom, and when she did, he seized her and demanded that she lie with him.

Tamar's answer is one of the clearest moral speeches in the book, and it deserves to stand in her own words. She refused him to his face: "No, my brother!" And then the law and the shame of it, in her own words: "Do not violate me, for such a thing should never be done in Israel. Do not do this disgraceful thing!" She argued shame, his and hers: where could she ever take her shame, and he would be counted among the fools in Israel. She even argued the desperate legal fiction available to her, that he should speak to the king, who would not withhold her from him. It was a better claim than the law allowed and it would not have saved her, but it shows a mind working at full speed for any exit. Amnon refused to listen to her, and being stronger than she was, he violated her. And then the verse that has chilled readers ever since, because it exposes what the desire had actually been: "Then Amnon hated Tamar with such intensity that his hatred was greater than the love he previously had." The love had never been love. He ordered her out, and when she protested that sending her away was a greater wrong than the wrong already done, a dismissal that branded her as the guilty party and closed every door of redress, he had his attendant throw her out and bolt the door behind her. Tamar was wearing the robe of many colors that marked the king's virgin daughters. She put ashes on her head, tore the robe, and went away crying aloud with her hand on her head, grief performed in the street because the law had been bolted inside.

Her brother Absalom found her and read the whole story at a glance, and his response was the coldest sentence in the chapter: be quiet for now, my sister; he is your brother; do not take this thing to heart. She obeyed, and lived as a desolate woman in Absalom's house, and the text will remember her name one more time, years later, when Absalom names his own beautiful daughter Tamar. King David heard all of it and was furious. The narrator records the fury and then, devastatingly, nothing after it: no trial, no punishment, no word. The king who had once exploded in righteous anger at Nathan's story of a stolen lamb did not summon Amnon, and the house of David learned what the king's silence licensed. Absalom learned it best. He never said a word to Amnon, either good or bad, because he hated him for violating his sister Tamar, and he waited two full years in silence while his father let the matter lie.

The blow fell at a sheepshearing feast at Baal-hazor, the same festive cover his father-by-crime had used for Uriah's war. Absalom invited all the king's sons, pressed a reluctant David to release Amnon, and ordered his servants to watch until Amnon's heart was merry with wine, and then to strike him down, and not to be afraid, because the command was his. They did as ordered, and every other prince fled on his mule, and the report that ran ahead of them to Jerusalem exaggerated as bad news does: Absalom had struck down all the sons of the king. David tore his clothes and lay on the ground, and it was Jonadab, the engineer of the original crime, who stepped forward with the correction, delivered with a shrewd man's perfect calm: only Amnon was dead, and Absalom had planned it since the day Amnon violated his sister. The other princes arrived wailing, and the court wept bitterly, and Absalom was gone, fled to his grandfather Talmai, king of Geshur, his mother's people, where he stayed three years. David mourned for his son every day, and in time he was consoled over Amnon's death and longed to go to Absalom. Absalom had done what David's justice had declined to do, and David's heart went after the murderer, which was also true.

What broke the exile was theater, arranged by Joab, who perceived that the king's heart longed for Absalom and decided, as ever, to manage his king. He fetched a wise woman from Tekoa and put words in her mouth: a widow, two sons, one dead by the other's hand in a field with no one to separate them, and now the clan demanded the surviving son's life for blood, which would extinguish her one remaining ember and cut off her husband's name from the earth. David rose to the case exactly as he had risen to Nathan's, and faster, swearing by the living LORD that not a hair of her son's head would fall to the ground. Then the woman turned the parable on its maker, as Nathan had taught this court that parables can turn: why had the king devised such a thing against the people of God, convicting himself by his own verdict, since he had not brought back his own banished son? Her ground was theology, and it is one of the great sentences in the book: "For we will surely die and be like water poured out on the ground, which cannot be recovered. Yet God does not take away a life, but He devises ways that the banished one may not be cast out from Him." David saw through the production in a single question, was Joab's hand behind this, and when she confessed it, he granted the request. Go, bring back the young man Absalom.

Bringing him back was where the reconciliation failed. Absalom returned to Jerusalem and to his own house, but the king's condition stood: he must not see my face. So the most praised man in Israel lived in the capital two full years in a restoration that restored nothing, father of three sons and of a daughter he named Tamar, famous for a beauty the narrator describes without a single flaw from sole to crown, famous also for the annual shearing of his hair, weighed out at two hundred shekels by the royal standard, a head of hair that this book wants you to remember. Shut out, Absalom sent for Joab twice and was twice refused, and then he did the arithmetic of a man who had learned in his father's house that only escalation gets an audience: he had his servants set Joab's barley field on fire. Joab came at once, demanding an explanation, and got the exile's whole case in one question: why had he come back from Geshur at all, when it would have been better to remain there? Let me see the king's face, Absalom said, and if there is iniquity in me, let him kill me. Joab carried it to David, and David summoned his son, and Absalom bowed facedown before the king, and the king kissed him. It reads like an ending. This book has taught you by now to count what is missing from its scenes of reunion: no confession was named, no crime was spoken, no dead were mentioned, and a kiss closed over two years of silence and a field of burned barley. Absalom walked out of his father's presence absolved of everything and reconciled to nothing, and he began, presently, to build a chariot.

title: The Rebellion
subtitle: 2 Samuel 15
description: Stolen hearts at the gate, a barefoot flight over Olivet, two counsels, and a prayer answered by delay.
paragraphs: After the kiss, Absalom built himself the equipment of a rival court: a chariot with horses and fifty men to run ahead of him, a rolling announcement that Israel had another address for its hopes. Then he worked the gate. He rose early and stood beside the road where every grievance in Israel came to petition the king, and he intercepted the petitioners before they ever reached David. Your claims are good and right, he would tell each one, but the king has no deputy to hear you. If only someone would appoint me judge in the land, then everyone with a dispute could come to me, and I would give him justice. And when a man approached to bow before the king's son, Absalom would stop the bow, take hold of the man, and kiss him, royal courtesy weaponized into intimacy. The narrator's verdict is a single plain sentence: in this way Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel. The raw material he worked with was real, and the book does not hide it. David's justice had grown remote inside his palace, the same palace where a sister's rape had gone unjudged and a murder had been answered with longing. Absalom did not manufacture the vacancy. He camped in it. Four years of this, and then the request that set the trap: permission to go to Hebron to pay a vow he claimed to have made in exile. David blessed him and sent him off with the words this family had used before a fall before. Go in peace. At Hebron the trumpets sounded across the tribes, Absalom reigns in Hebron, and two hundred guests who had come innocently from Jerusalem found themselves exhibits in a coronation. And the conspiracy gained strength, because Absalom had sent for the one man whose counsel was treated in those days like an oracle of God: Ahithophel the Gilonite, David's counselor. The text never explains his defection. It gives one thread and leaves it visible: Bathsheba's father Eliam stands in the roster of David's mighty men as a son of Ahithophel the Gilonite. The wisest man in Israel was the grandfather of the woman on the roof, and he went over to the rebellion with his counsel intact.

The messenger's report to David was six words of summary: the hearts of the men of Israel are with Absalom. David's decision was instant and it was the decision of the fugitive of twenty years before, not of a king defending a throne: arise and let us flee, or we will not escape. He left ten concubines to keep the palace, a detail the story is not finished with, and the court streamed out of the city eastward, past the last house, across the Kidron, toward the wilderness, while the countryside wept loudly at the sight. The book slows the procession down to name its loyalists, and the naming matters. The king's foreign bodyguard marched past, Cherethites and Pelethites and six hundred Gittites, Philistines who had followed him from Gath, and David stopped their commander, Ittai, a foreigner and an exile who had arrived only yesterday, and released him from any obligation: go back, stay with the new king. Ittai's answer is the covenant loyalty of Jonathan translated into a soldier's oath: "As surely as the LORD lives, and as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king may be, whether it means life or death, there will your servant be!" A man from Gath swore to David in exile what Israel at the gate would not. Then came Zadok and Abiathar with the ark on the Levites' shoulders, and David sent the ark back into the city, in the anti-climax of his entire career: no talisman this time, no carrying God into his emergency. "If I find favor in the eyes of the LORD, He will bring me back and let me see both it and His dwelling place again." And if the verdict went the other way, if God should say of him, "I do not delight in you", David's answer was already settled: "here I am; let Him do to me whatever seems good to Him". He submits to a verdict he has not heard, from the God who had already forgiven him a capital sin and kept the sentence standing. The priests went back as his eyes in the city, their sons as runners, and David climbed the Mount of Olives weeping, head covered, barefoot, while everyone with him covered their heads and wept as they went. The Psalter preserves a song for this slope: Psalm 3 carries the heading, a psalm of David, when he fled from his son Absalom. At the summit, where David used to worship, two pieces of news arrived in sequence. First, that Ahithophel was among the conspirators, and David prayed the shortest prayer of his life, asking God to turn Ahithophel's counsel into foolishness. Second, Hushai the Archite, his friend, robe torn and dust on his head, and David, thinking faster than his grief, sent him back into the city as the answer to that prayer: go, present yourself as Absalom's servant, and defeat the counsel of Ahithophel from inside the room.

On the far side of the summit the fugitives met supply and slander in the same hour. Ziba came down with loaded donkeys, two hundred loaves, raisins, summer fruit, wine, a steward's perfect instincts on full display, and the king asked where his master was. Ziba's report was short: Mephibosheth was staying in Jerusalem, because he had said that today the house of Israel would restore to him his grandfather's kingdom. David, exhausted, betrayed by his son that week, believed the servant's word about the lame man he had seated at his table, and on the spot he transferred everything Mephibosheth owned to Ziba. The book does not tell you yet whether Ziba lied. It files the grant and moves on, leaving a king's hasty sentence in wartime to be weighed later, when the king comes back over this same road and two men tell two stories. Around the next bend waited Shimei son of Gera, of Saul's family, at Bahurim, and he came out cursing and throwing stones at the king and his mighty men, dust in the air, shouting that the LORD had paid David back for all the blood of the house of Saul, and delivered the kingdom to Absalom, and that David had come to ruin because he was a man of bloodshed. Some of the charge was false: David had shed no blood of Saul's house, and had executed the men who did. Some of it landed nearer than David's guards could admit, on a road away from a city where a Hittite's blood was still unaccounted for. Abishai asked leave to cross over and take the head off this dead dog. David refused, and his reasoning is the theological center of the flight: if Shimei cursed because the LORD had told him to curse David, then who could ask the man, "Why did you do this?" His own son, his flesh and blood, sought his life; how much more this Benjamite. Leave him alone. "Perhaps the LORD will see my affliction and repay me with good for the cursing I receive today." So the king walked on under the stones, and Shimei kept pace along the ridge, cursing and throwing dust, until the company reached the Jordan, exhausted, and refreshed themselves there.

In Jerusalem, the rebellion crowned itself with an act of policy. Hushai arrived as Absalom entered the city and survived his first interview with a courtier's nerve, swearing loyalty to the one chosen by the LORD and by Israel. Then Absalom asked Ahithophel what to do, and Ahithophel's first counsel was not military. Sleep with your father's concubines, the ones he left to keep the palace, in the sight of all Israel: it would make Absalom a stench to his father beyond reconciliation, and strengthen every hand that had joined him. They pitched a tent on the roof, the same roof in this story's architecture, and Absalom went in to his father's concubines before the eyes of the nation, and Nathan's sentence, given in a quiet room years before, fulfilled itself clause by clause: what David had done in secret was answered in broad daylight before all Israel. Ahithophel's second counsel was the war itself, and it was perfect: twelve thousand men, tonight, while David was weak and weary; strike only the king; the people would scatter and could then be brought back like a bride to her husband, with the life of one man the whole cost. It pleased Absalom and every elder in the room. Then Absalom, on an impulse the book attributes at the deepest level to God's purpose, asked to hear Hushai as well. Hushai's counter-counsel was flattery built into strategy: this time, he said, Ahithophel's advice was not sound. David was a man of war, fierce as a bear robbed of her cubs, and he would not be sleeping with the troops; a first bloody check would melt Israel's courage. Instead, gather all Israel from Dan to Beersheba, a multitude like the sand on the seashore, and let Absalom himself lead them down on David like dew, until not one man remained. Absalom and all the men of Israel chose Hushai's counsel, and the narrator steps out from behind the story to tell you why the worse plan won: "For the LORD had purposed to thwart the good counsel of Ahithophel in order to bring disaster on Absalom." The prayer on the Mount of Olives had been answered inside the enemy's council chamber, by delay.

Delay was all David needed. The priests' sons ran the warning out of the city by a servant girl's errand, hid in a well in a Bahurim courtyard under a covering scattered with grain while Absalom's men searched above them, and reached the king: cross the Jordan tonight. By daybreak there was no one left who had not crossed. And Ahithophel, reading the rejection of his counsel as the verdict it was, saddled his donkey, rode home to Giloh, put his affairs in order, and hanged himself, and was buried in his father's tomb, the counselor of Israel exiting the story with the same cold competence he had brought to it. David reached Mahanaim, where Saul's pretender had once been crowned, and found the country rallying to the fugitive as it had in the old days: Shobi from Rabbah, Machir of Lo-debar, the same man who had sheltered Mephibosheth, and Barzillai the Gileadite brought beds and basins and wheat and beans and honey and cheese to the camp, because they said the people had become hungry and exhausted and thirsty in the wilderness. Absalom crossed the Jordan after him with all Israel, having set Amasa, Joab's own cousin, over his army in Joab's place. The two hosts stood in Gilead, and the rebellion moved toward the forest of Ephraim.

title: The Forest of Ephraim, and a Father's Cry
subtitle: 2 Samuel 18
description: Twenty thousand in the forest, a king between two gates, a hard return, and Sheba's trumpet.
paragraphs: David reviewed his troops at Mahanaim and divided them in thirds, under Joab, under Abishai, and under Ittai the Gittite, the foreigner of a week's loyalty now commanding a third of the kingdom's army. The king announced that he would march out with them himself, and the army talked him out of it on grounds that were love and arithmetic at once: if they fled, no one would care; if half of them died, no one would care; but David was worth ten thousand of them, and the enemy's whole war was one man's death. So David stood beside the gate while the army marched out by hundreds and by thousands, and in the hearing of every commander and, the text is careful to say, of all the people, he gave the order that frames the day: "Treat the young man Absalom gently for my sake." Then the battle was joined in the forest of Ephraim, and the slaughter was great, twenty thousand men, and the battle spread over the whole countryside, and the narrator delivers the day's epitaph in a sentence no historian would dare invent: that day the forest devoured more people than the sword.

Absalom the forest took personally. Riding his mule through the trees in the rout, he met some of David's servants, and as the mule passed under the thick branches of a large oak, his head was caught fast in the tree, and the mule kept going, and the king's son hung suspended in midair. The book had once paused a whole paragraph over that head, the flawless beauty of it, the hair sheared yearly and weighed at two hundred shekels; now the head is the snare. A soldier saw him hanging and reported it to Joab, and Joab's response tells you the war he thought he was fighting: why had the man not struck Absalom to the ground on the spot; there would have been ten shekels of silver and a warrior's belt in it. The soldier's refusal is the moral summit of the chapter. Even if a thousand shekels were weighed into his hands, he said, he would not raise his hand against the son of the king, because in their hearing the king had commanded Joab and Abishai and Ittai: "Protect the young man Absalom for my sake." And he added the clause that measured Joab exactly: if he had done it and betrayed his own life, nothing being hidden from the king, Joab would have abandoned him. Joab announced that he was not going to wait like this, took three spears in his hand, and thrust them through the heart of Absalom while he was still alive in the oak. Ten of Joab's armor-bearers finished it. The trumpet blew, the pursuit stopped, and they took Absalom down and threw him into a large pit in the forest and piled a huge mound of stones over him, the burial of an executed criminal. In his lifetime Absalom had set up a pillar for himself in the King's Valley near Jerusalem, because he said he had no son to preserve the memory of his name, though this same book records three sons born to him and does not stop to explain the difference. The pillar still stands in the telling with his name on it. The man is under stones in a pit, in a forest, unwept by the army that marched home without him.

David sat between the two gates of Mahanaim waiting for the news, and the book slows down to the pace of a watchman's eyes. A runner alone: good news, said the king, if he is alone, he bears good news. A second runner behind him. The watchman recognized the first man's stride, Ahimaaz son of Zadok, and David said he was a good man and came with good news. Ahimaaz had begged Joab for the run over Joab's refusal, Joab knowing precisely what the news would do to the king, and the young priest arrived crying that all was well, and blessed the LORD who had delivered up the men who raised their hands against the king. Then David asked the only question he had asked all day: "Is the young man Absalom all right?" Ahimaaz, who knew, chose a fog: when Joab sent him he had seen a great tumult, but he did not know what it was. The king told him to step aside, and the Cushite came, the foreign messenger Joab had sent first with the whole truth, and delivered it in the formula of victories. David asked him the same question, and the Cushite answered with a courtier's terrible precision: "May the enemies of my lord the king and all who rise up against you to harm you be like that young man." The king was shaken. He went up to the chamber over the gate and wept, and as he walked he cried out the words that have never stopped echoing: "O my son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! If only I had died instead of you, O Absalom, my son, my son!" The kingdom had been saved in a day. The victory was total. And the king's grief filled the gatehouse where the whole army would have to pass under it.

It turned the victory into mourning for all the people. The army that had saved the king's life and throne came back into the city quietly, stealing in like men humiliated after a rout, while the king covered his face and cried the lament at the top of his voice. Then Joab went in to him, the indispensable, unforgivable commander, and performed the last service of his brutal loyalty: he shamed the king back onto his throne. Today, he said, David had disgraced the servants who had saved his life and his family's lives. "You love those who hate you and hate those who love you!" He had made it plain that commanders and soldiers meant nothing to him, and had Absalom lived and all of them died, it would have pleased him. Then the warning, sworn by the LORD: "if you do not go out, not a man will remain with you tonight", and that would be worse than all the adversity of his life from his youth until now. Every word of the rebuke was insubordinate and every word was true, and the king heard it. He rose, washed the grief off his public face, and sat in the gate, and all the people came before him. A king could mourn his son. He could not invoice his army for the mourning.

The restoration that followed was a second coronation conducted in arguments. Israel, Absalom dead, remembered David's rescues and began asking why no one spoke of restoring the king. David moved first on Judah, his own tribe, asking through the priests why his brothers should be last to bring him home, and he sweetened the summons with a political appointment that would cost more blood: Amasa, Absalom's commander, his own nephew, was to be commander of the army from now on in place of Joab. Judah came down to the Jordan as one man, and at the crossing the whole tangled past queued up to be settled. Shimei came first, a thousand Benjamites behind him, fell before the king, confessed his sin and begged that it not be held against him, and Abishai asked why this man who had cursed the LORD's anointed should not die, and David answered in the idiom of a king secure enough for mercy: should any man be put to death in Israel today? "Am I not indeed aware that today I am king over Israel?" And to Shimei he swore an oath: "You shall not die." Then Mephibosheth came down, and his appearance testified before he spoke: he had not cared for his feet or trimmed his mustache or washed his clothes from the day the king left until the day he returned. His account contradicted Ziba's in every particular. Being lame, he had ordered his donkey saddled to ride with the king; his servant had deceived him, and then slandered him to the king in his absence. The king, the text observes, was like the angel of God to do what was good in his eyes. David cut the hearing short, why say any more, and split the estate between them, a king's compromise that decided everything except the truth. Mephibosheth's answer closes his story with the grace that had first brought him to the table: "let Ziba take it all", since his lord the king had come safely to his own house. Last came Barzillai, eighty years old, who had provisioned the court at Mahanaim, invited now to live out his days fed at the king's side in Jerusalem. His refusal is the gentlest speech in the book: how many years had he left that he should go up with the king? At eighty, could he discern what was good and what was not, could he taste what he ate or drank, could he still hear the voices of singing men and women? Why should your servant be an added burden to my lord the king? He crossed a little way over the Jordan, commended his son Chimham to the king's generosity, received David's kiss and blessing, and went home to die near the tomb of his father and mother.

Even restored, the kingdom cracked along its oldest seam in the homeward crowd itself, Israel charging Judah with stealing the king, Judah answering with kinship and insult, until at the river's far end a Benjamite named Sheba son of Bichri blew the ram's horn and shouted the slogan that would outlive David's house: "We have no share in David, no inheritance in Jesse's son. Every man to his tent, O Israel!" Israel deserted to Sheba, and Judah escorted its king home to a palace where the ten concubines were taken and placed in a guarded house, provided for and never visited again, confined until the day of their death, living as widows, the human residue of a sentence pronounced in a prophet's quiet room. Amasa, given three days to muster Judah, missed his deadline, and David sent the pursuit under Abishai, fearing Sheba would do more harm than Absalom. At the great stone in Gibeon, Amasa joined the column, and Joab came forward to greet his replacement, dressed for war with a dagger strapped that slipped conveniently from its sheath. "Are you well, my brother?" he asked, and took Amasa by the beard with his right hand to kiss him, and with the other drove the dagger into his stomach, and Amasa wallowed in his blood in the middle of the road while the army halted around the body until a man dragged it aside and covered it, because no column could march past it. It was Abner again, and Asahel's blood again, and David nowhere in the scene, the king's appointment undone by the king's uncommandable commander. Joab pursued Sheba to Abel-beth-maacah at the kingdom's northern edge and battered the wall, and there the revolt was ended not by Joab but by a wise woman calling down from the city, the second wise woman of the book, who named her city a mother in Israel and asked why Joab would swallow up the LORD's inheritance. Joab disclaimed any wish to destroy; deliver Sheba alone, and he would depart. "his head will be thrown to you over the wall", she promised, and she went to her people with her wise counsel, and it was. The trumpet blew, the army dispersed home, and Joab returned to Jerusalem and to the post the chapter's final list confirms as if nothing had happened: Joab was over the whole army of Israel. David was king again over a united kingdom, and the sons of Zeruiah remained, as he had confessed a lifetime earlier, too fierce for him.

title: The Last Things
subtitle: 2 Samuel 21
description: A famine and a mother's vigil, the great song, the honor roll, and a threshing floor bought at full price.
paragraphs: The last four chapters of this book are not the next four things that happened. They are the book's appendix, gathered out of sequence the way the closing chapters of Judges were gathered, a famine from somewhere in the reign's middle, battles from its wars, a song from the day of deliverance looking back over everything, and a plague near the end. Read them as the author's final exhibits, set side by side so that the reign can be weighed whole.

The first exhibit is a famine, three successive years of it, and David sought the face of the LORD, and the answer was a blood debt inside the national past: "It is because of the blood shed by Saul and his family, because he killed the Gibeonites." The Gibeonites were the people who had tricked Israel into a covenant in Joshua's day, and Israel had sworn to them before God, and the oath had held for centuries, until Saul, in his zeal for Israel and Judah, tried to exterminate them. A dead king's zeal had become a living land's drought. David summoned the Gibeonites and asked what he could do, how he could make amends so that they might bless the inheritance of the LORD. They refused silver and gold; money was not the currency of this debt. For the man who had consumed them and plotted to wipe them from every border of Israel, they asked seven of his male descendants, to be hanged before the LORD at Gibeah of Saul. David gave them. The covenant with Jonathan fenced off one name first: the king spared Mephibosheth because of the oath between them. The seven taken were two sons of Rizpah, Saul's concubine, the same woman whose treatment by Abner had once cracked the house of Saul open, and five sons of Saul's daughter Merab. They were hanged on the hill in the first days of the barley harvest, all seven together, and then their mother did the thing this appendix is remembered for. Rizpah took sackcloth and spread it on a rock and kept vigil over the bodies from the beginning of harvest until the rains came, months on a rock, driving the birds from them by day and the beasts by night, a concubine of a fallen house performing with her own body the honor that nations had refused her sons. When David was told what she had done, he went and gathered the bones of Saul and Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead, who had rescued them from the square at Beth-shan a generation before, and the bones of the hanged men with them, and buried them all together in the tomb of Saul's father Kish. After they had done everything the king commanded, the text says, "God answered their prayers for the land." The famine ends not with the executions but with the burial, and it is Rizpah's vigil that moves the king to it. The book keeps its pattern to the end: God hears, and the lowly are the ones who show the king his duty.

The second exhibit is David's strength running out. The Philistines came to war again, and David went down with his men and fought, and became exhausted, and a giant named Ishbi-benob, with a bronze spearhead of three hundred shekels and a new sword, resolved to kill him, and would have, had Abishai not come to his aid and struck the Philistine down. Then David's men swore an oath of their own to their king: "You must never again go out with us to battle, so that the lamp of Israel may not be extinguished." The shepherd who ran toward Goliath was now the treasure the army refused to spend. Three more battles against the giants of Gath follow in a rapid honor roll: Saph, killed by Sibbecai; a second giant at Gob killed by Elhanan of Bethlehem, whom this text names as the killer of the brother of Goliath the Gittite, a reading the Chronicles account shares, whatever older tellings made of it; and a taunting giant with six fingers on each hand and six toes on each foot, killed by Jonathan, David's nephew. Four descendants of Rapha fell, the text concludes, at the hands of David and his servants. The giant-killing that began with one boy and a sling had become the house trade.

Then the appendix sets down its centerpiece: the song. David sang it, the heading says, on the day the LORD delivered him from all his enemies and from the hand of Saul, and the same song stands in the Psalter as Psalm 18, one song with two addresses, in the king's story and in the nation's worship. It opens with a pile of names for God heaped like stones: "The LORD is my rock, my fortress, and my deliverer." It remembers drowning, the waves of death and the cords of Sheol, and the cry that reached God's temple, and then it remembers rescue as the sky tearing open, God coming down with dark clouds under His feet, thundering, scattering enemies with arrows of lightning, reaching down from on high to draw one man out of deep waters. "He brought me out into the open; He rescued me because He delighted in me." It is the old man's theology of his own survival, and he states its principle without embarrassment: God deals with people as they deal with Him, faithful to the faithful, and it remembers what God made of him, feet like a deer on the heights, arms trained to bend a bow of bronze. "For You, O LORD, are my lamp; the LORD lights up my darkness." And the song ends where chapter 7 began it, on the covenant, the forever promise now worn smooth by a lifetime of testing: "He shows loving devotion to His anointed, to David and his descendants forever."

Beside the song stand the last words, and beside them the honor roll. The last words call David the oracle of the man raised on high, the anointed of the God of Jacob, the sweet psalmist of Israel, and they define the king he had tried and failed and tried to be: "He who rules the people with justice, who rules in the fear of God, is like the light of the morning at sunrise of a cloudless dawn". And they rest, at the end, not on the reign's record but on the covenant: "For He has established with me an everlasting covenant, ordered and secured in every part." Then come the mighty men, the Thirty and the Three above them: Josheb-basshebeth, who killed eight hundred at one time; Eleazar, who fought until his hand froze to his sword; Shammah, who held a lentil field alone while Israel fled. There is the story of the three who broke through the Philistine garrison at Bethlehem to bring David water he had longed for aloud, and David, who would not drink it, who poured it out to the LORD saying, "Is this not the blood of the men who risked their lives?" There is Benaiah, who killed a lion in a pit on a day of snow. And the roll closes, in the book's last accounting of honor, with the name it can neither promote nor omit: and Uriah the Hittite. Thirty-seven in all.

The final exhibit is a sin of the king's old age, and this book's last word about power. The anger of the LORD burned against Israel, and David was stirred to count the fighting men, a census Joab and the commanders were sent to execute from Dan to Beersheba. Remarkably, it is Joab who protests, Joab of the bloody hands and the unerring instinct for what a king should not be seen doing: "But why does my lord the king want to do such a thing?" The king's word prevailed. Nine months and twenty days the counters walked the land, and the totals came back, eight hundred thousand in Israel and five hundred thousand in Judah, an empire numbered like property. And after he had numbered the troops, David's conscience was stricken, the same conviction that had once struck him over a corner of a robe, and he confessed in the old plain words: "I have sinned greatly in what I have done. Now, O LORD, I beg You to take away the iniquity of Your servant, for I have acted very foolishly." The word of the LORD came through Gad the prophet with a choice of sentences, three years of famine, three months of flight before enemies, or three days of plague, and David chose with the last great act of theological judgment in the book: "I am deeply distressed. Please, let us fall into the hand of the LORD, for His mercies are great; but do not let me fall into the hands of men." The plague fell, and seventy thousand died from Dan to Beersheba, and as the angel stretched out his hand toward Jerusalem the LORD relented and spoke the mercy David had banked on: "Enough! Withdraw your hand now!" The angel stood at the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite. David, seeing the angel, made the intercession of a shepherd king and reversed Uriah's account at last: the sin was his, the sheep had done nothing; let God's hand fall on him and his father's house. Gad sent him up to build an altar on that threshing floor, and Araunah came out bowing and offered everything as a gift, oxen and sledges and yokes. The king refused the gift with the sentence that ends his story's account of worship: "I insist on paying a price, for I will not offer to the LORD my God burnt offerings that cost me nothing." He bought the floor and the oxen for fifty shekels of silver, built the altar, offered the sacrifices, and the plague was halted, and the LORD answered the prayers on behalf of the land. The book of David does not end in the palace or on a battlefield. It ends on a purchased threshing floor above the city, where the king paid full price to stand between his people and judgment. The story will say later what that ground became. David's own book leaves him there, at an altar, in the last place his sin and God's mercy ever met.
